title: Electrically Tunable Two-Component Exciton Condensate in a Coulomb-Coupled Graphene Trilayer
authors: Bo Zou, A. Okounkova, Shuaiqing Zhang, Jian Liao, J. Pack, K. Watanabe, T. Taniguchi, Yihang Zeng
abstract: Multicomponent condensates possess internal phase degrees of freedom unavailable to a single-component condensate, yet their components are rarely controllable in solids. Here we realize a graphene trilayer with negligible interlayer tunnelling in which the layer-specific carrier densities are continuously tuned by electrostatic gating. Quantum-capacitance measurements demonstrate that charge-incompressible quantum Hall states at total filling factors 1 and 2 persist across the full range of layer-filling configurations and continuously connect the three bilayer exciton-condensate limits. This persistence provides evidence for a trilayer excitonic state. Static Hartree-Fock and time-dependent Hartree-Fock calculations yield two independent finite phase-stiffness eigenmodes and two linearly dispersing Goldstone modes, respectively, when all three layers are partially filled, whereas only one phase-stiffness eigenmode and one linear Goldstone mode remain when one layer is unfilled. The stiffness eigenmodes rotate continuously between the two adjacent-layer exciton bases as charge is transferred among the layers, revealing electrical control of the condensate-mode composition. Together, the experimental and theoretical results support the identification of a two-component exciton condensate with a continuously tunable internal structure.
summary: This work reports on the realization of an electrically tunable two-component exciton condensate in a graphene trilayer. By combining quantum capacitance measurements with advanced mean-field theory, the authors demonstrate that the condensate's internal structure can be continuously controlled by electrostatic gating. This provides strong evidence for a highly controllable, correlated excitonic phase in solid-state matter.
main_problem: To realize and study the continuously tunable internal structure of a two-component exciton condensate in a solid-state system, moving beyond systems where component properties are fixed by material chemistry.
main_result: The experiment confirms the existence of a two-component exciton condensate with a continuously tunable internal structure, supported by the observation of persistent quantum Hall states and the continuous rotation of condensate mode composition.
method: The study combines quantum-capacitance measurements (experimental) with Hartree-Fock and Time-Dependent Hartree-Fock calculations (theoretical) to analyze collective excitations.
model_or_system: The system is a graphene trilayer with negligible interlayer tunneling, supporting excitons bound by Coulomb interaction. The condensate is modeled as having two independent relative U(1) symmetries.

main_assumptions: The analysis assumes negligible single-particle tunneling between layers and relies on mean-field approximations (Hartree-Fock).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate schematics of single- and two-component condensates, quantum capacitance measurements showing QHS states, and 3D scans mapping incompressibility across the layer-filling space.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical platform and experimental control, uses quantum capacitance to map out incompressible states, and then employs theoretical calculations (HF/TDHF) to characterize the resulting two-component condensate modes and their continuous tunability.
why_interesting: The ability to electrically tune the internal structure of a correlated quantum state (the exciton condensate) provides a clean platform to study the interplay between external control parameters and emergent many-body symmetries, relevant to understanding correlated phases in artificial lattices.
